getAbout.title: About
getAbout.name: Cristopher Cervantes
getAbout.headline: Engineering Manager & Tech Lead. Nine years of shipping software from a beach town in Baja to people all over the world.
getAbout.summary: Engineering Manager and Tech Lead with 9+ years building production software. At PSL Group I grew from Senior Application Developer to running engineering for FirstWord, DGPL, MEC and AMI. Before that: payroll and attendance software for three countries, and factory software that doubled a plant's output.
getAbout.description:
I'm 32 and I'm from Rosarito, Baja California, a beach town just south of Tijuana. My first production code ran at the border, and 9+ years later the things I build are used by people I'll never meet, in countries I've never been to.

I didn't show up knowing much. I was an intern who could barely scratch out a few lines of code, and I got better one job at a time, until I was one of the people the team leaned on at every company I joined.

These days I'm half Engineering Manager, half Tech Lead. I set the priorities, run the 1:1s and plan the roadmap, and I still open pull requests and leave long comments on other people's. When I push back on a design I bring another way to do it, because a no on its own doesn't teach anybody anything.

Off the clock I'm working out, with my family, or every now and then a few volumes deep into a manga or a video game. A few of those games left relics hidden around this page. Good luck.

highlights: Algorithms, databases, networks and more late nights than I'd like to count. Most of what I still lean on started here.
Part of TecNM, Mexico's national network of public engineering schools.

getSkills.title: Leading Teams
getSkills.description: My calendar is mostly 1:1s, and I like it that way. I'd rather unblock five engineers before lunch than write the clever thing myself.
getSkills.effect: Once per sprint: every engineer on your side of the field is unblocked.

getSkills.title: AI & LLMs
getSkills.description: Models get things wrong, so I treat them like any other dependency: guardrails, tests and a fallback. A boring right answer beats a brilliant wrong one.
getSkills.effect: When a model hallucinates, negate it and return a grounded answer instead.

getSkills.title: Cloud & Infra
getSkills.description: Functions when traffic spikes, containers when it doesn't, and nothing clicked together by hand in a console. If it isn't in code, it doesn't exist.
getSkills.effect: Cannot be destroyed by a Friday deploy.

getSkills.title: Frontend & UX
getSkills.description: Component libraries a whole product can share, and the small stuff people only notice when it's missing: loading states, dark mode, copy that sounds like a person.
getSkills.effect: Flip every loading spinner on the field into a skeleton.

getSkills.title: Data & Search
getSkills.description: I start from how the data will be read and work backwards. Documents when the access patterns are known, tables when the relationships matter, an index when people need answers fast.
getSkills.effect: Search your deck for any record and add it to your hand. Indexed, of course.

getSkills.title: Quality & Security
getSkills.description: Unit tests for the logic, end to end tests for the paths people actually click, and a CI that's allowed to say no. Secrets and alerts go in before launch, not after the first 3 a.m. page.
getSkills.effect: Negate any attack that skipped CI.

getCaseStudies.title: FirstWord AI
getCaseStudies.summary: Claude agents on AWS Bedrock that answer questions about the medical news FirstWord publishes.
getCaseStudies.challenge: FirstWord's readers make real decisions on what they read. An assistant that sounds sure and gets it wrong would cost more trust than it could ever earn.
approach: Versioned every agent, so a prompt or model change ships and rolls back like any other release
Streamed answers to the reader while the model is still writing, nobody stares at a spinner
Put guardrails in front of every response, and kept the model honest with tests
getCaseStudies.outcome: An assistant that lives inside the product readers already open every day, not off to the side of it.

getCaseStudies.title: FirstWord Manager
getCaseStudies.summary: The workspace the FirstWord team runs its day from, with the information in one place and the busywork on autopilot.
getCaseStudies.challenge: What the team needed lived across several tools, and a good part of every week went to repeating the same steps by hand.
approach: Built FirstWord Manager in Next.js, the one workspace the team runs everything from
Centralized the information that was spread across tools, so everyone works from the same source
Automated the processes the team used to run by hand
getCaseStudies.outcome: Less time hunting for data and repeating steps, more time on the work that actually moves FirstWord forward.

getCaseStudies.title: Pipelines every team ships through
getCaseStudies.summary: One road to production for every repo, plus the Claude Code setup the whole team works with.
getCaseStudies.challenge: Every repo deployed its own way, which made releases slow to review and nerve wracking to press.
approach: Moved the environments into infrastructure as code
Wrote shared GitHub Actions workflows that every repo reuses instead of copying
Set up Claude Code and the conventions around it, so the team gets help without losing its own style
getCaseStudies.outcome: A new repo is ready to ship on day one, through the same reviewed path as every other.

getCaseStudies.title: GTI B2 and facial terminals
getCaseStudies.summary: Attendance terminals, including facial ones, that Tress customers leaned on to keep track of their people through the pandemic.
getCaseStudies.challenge: Companies still needed to know who was at work, in the middle of a pandemic.
approach: Built the GTI B2 terminals, and then the facial terminals that followed them
getCaseStudies.outcome: Some of the first tools Tress customers had for personnel control during the pandemic.

getCaseStudies.title: GTI Controls
getCaseStudies.summary: The React component library under Interis Works, Tress's cloud payroll product.
getCaseStudies.challenge: Several teams were building one product, and you could tell which team built which screen.
approach: Built one shared library of React components for the whole product
Gave every team the same building blocks for forms, tables and layouts
getCaseStudies.outcome: You can no longer tell which team built which screen, which was the whole point.

getCaseStudies.title: A plant that doubled its output
getCaseStudies.summary: Software that talked straight to the factory robots, and took a whole plant's productivity up 100%.
getCaseStudies.challenge: Material, people and machines on the plant floor were coordinated by hand, and it showed in the numbers.
approach: Designed automated processes that talk directly to the plant's robotics
Added material access and personnel control to the same system
Built a Jira style ticketing app so the IT team could stop living in email
